paper_title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Tabular data are widely used in biomedical machine learning, representing structured information in electronic health records (EHR), genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, drug discovery, and single-cell studies. These datasets support predictive tasks critical to clinical decision-making and biological discovery [1, 2]. Despite the success of modern machine learning methods, including gradientboosted decision trees, deep neural networks, and emerging tabular foundation models (TFMs), systematic comparisons in biomedical prediction settings remain fragmented and inconsistent. Recent benchmarking efforts have improved the reproducibility and systematic evaluation of tabular models [3]. In particular, TabArena [4] puts emphasis on standardized evaluation pipelines, careful dataset curation, and continuous benchmarking. However, existing benchmarks are designed largely for general-purpose tabular data and do not systematically capture the unique challenges of biomedical *These authors contributed equally to this work. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets. Figure 1: TabBioMed overview across eight biomedical domains and four model families. The UpSet plot summarizes which model families appear among the top five models for each dataset. Horizontal bars on the left show the total number of datasets in which each family is represented. Connected dots indicate the exact combination of families represented among the top five models for each dataset, while the stacked bars above show the number of datasets exhibiting that combination, stratified by biomedical domain. datasets, which often exhibit widely varying sample sizes and feature dimensionalities [5, 6], pervasive missingness [7], class imbalance, and modality-specific measurement processes [8]. Consequently, the conclusions of the existing benchmarks may not transfer directly to many biomedical applications. Prior studies have compared neural networks, gradient-boosted decision trees [9, 10], and more recently tabular foundation models [11], but primarily on non-biomedical datasets. As result, there remains no comprehensive benchmark spanning the full range of biomedical regimes. In this work, we address this gap through TabBioMed,1 large-scale benchmark suite for biomedical tabular machine learning. Our main contributions are: (i) large-scale biomedical dataset curation, comprising 94 biomedical tabular datasets across eight domains, including EHR, genomics, transcriptomics, drug discovery and molecular properties, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology, (ii) unified preprocessing framework, with standardized but flexible pipeline that preserves domain-specific structure while enabling fair and reproducible comparisons, (iii) comprehensive model evaluation, benchmarking 23 models spanning linear methods, gradientboosted decision trees, deep tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models, and (iv) robust benchmarking protocol, providing standardized evaluation across datasets, models, and data regimes to support reliable large-scale benchmarking in biomedical machine learning. We analyze how model families behave across domains (Figure 1), how predictive performance relates to computational efficiency, and how dataset characteristics influence performance variation. Tabular foundation models emerge as the strongest predictive family, although this advantage reflects familylevel performance rather than uniform superiority of individual models. Missing evaluations occur more frequently for foundation models on larger, high-dimensional datasets due to computational constraints, but sensitivity analyses show that the main ranking trends remain under complete-case analysis and missing-score imputation. Under limited computational budgets, tree-based methods and well-tuned multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) remain highly competitive and often preferable. Overall, our analysis shows that performance is highly regime-dependent. Rather than identifying universally optimal method, the benchmark highlights systematic variation across datasets, domains, and computational constraints, supporting more informed and dataset-aware model selection. 1https://huggingface.co/spaces/TabBioMed

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: The tabular machine learning community has developed numerous benchmark suites to evaluate predictive models on structured data. As summarized in Table 1, these benchmarks vary widely in their scale, dataset size regimes, and curation procedures. Large-scale collections such as PMLB [12], TALENT [13, 14], and TabRepo [15] prioritize breadth, offering hundreds of datasets across diverse domains to capture wide array of learning scenarios. Conversely, efforts like OpenML-CC18 [16], TabZilla [10], and TabArena [4] employ more selective dataset curation strategies, often distilling hundreds of candidates down to high-quality, medium-sized subsets. Other suites address specific data regimes, such as TabReD [17], which targets industry-scale datasets. Despite this progress, there is no single large-scale benchmark for tabular biomedical data that matches the scope of these general-purpose suites. Instead, biomedical datasets remain scattered as incidental subsets within broader multi-domain collections, which limits their utility for healthcare and biological settings due to lack of domain-specific standardization. Although there are domain-specific benchmarks and comparative studies, such as MoleculeNet [18] for molecular property prediction, MLOmics [19] for cancer multi-omics, tree-based and linear model comparison for biobank phenotype prediction [20], and comparative studies of machine learning methods on metabolomics datasets [21, 22], they remain focused on particular biomedical domains or task families and do not provide unified evaluation framework in biomedical settings. Furthermore, exhaustive benchmarking on massive general-purpose suites can quickly become computationally prohibitive. For instance, the TabArena authors estimate total of 15 wall-clock years for their experiments without parallelization [4]. Through TabBioMed, we address these gaps with 94 curated datasets, balancing biomedical breadth with tractable, standardized evaluation protocol. Table 1: Benchmark comparison. sections.title: 3 TabBioMed Benchmark
sections.content: TabBioMed is large-scale benchmark of heterogeneous biomedical structured prediction tasks. We next describe its dataset curation, preprocessing, and evaluation protocol. 3 3.1 Datasets Dataset Curation. We focus on biomedical classification and regression tasks based on clinical variables, omics measurements, and engineered molecular or sequence features. These datasets are represented as sample-by-feature tables. We exclude tasks requiring native sequence, image, graph, or temporal modeling. While some datasets exhibit dependencies across samples (e.g., repeated measurements per patient or batch effects), we do not assume that samples are independent. Instead, we use dataset-specific splitting protocols, including group-aware and scaffold-aware splits where appropriate. Figure 2 summarizes the resulting benchmark. Figure 2: TabBioMed Benchmark Datasets. Distribution of datasets across task types, biomedical domains, and data sources, along with the relationship between dataset size and feature dimensionality. Dataset Unification and Preprocessing. Raw datasets are converted into common representation consisting of feature matrix X, target array y, and metadata describing task type, dataset statistics, and split information. general validation stage checks data integrity, normalizes labels where needed, and verifies schema consistency. Model-specific imputation, encoding, and scaling are deferred to training. Dataset-specific details appear in Appendix A. consolidated curation flow appears in Figure 7. Splitting Strategy. Evaluation splits are assigned during dataset preparation and stored in metadata. Datasets with 500 samples use 5-fold cross-validation by default, with stratification for classification when possible. Larger datasets use predefined dataset-specific splits when available, otherwise 70/15/15 train/validation/test splits. Dataset-specific protocols take precedence over these defaults. They include grouped cross-validation and group-aware or scaffold-aware fixed splits, preserving the designated groups across partitions. 3.2 Models and Hyperparameter Optimization We benchmark 23 models across four families: classical baselines, tree-based models, neural tabular models, and tabular foundation models  (Table 12)  . Classical baselines comprise LinearModel, LassoModel [26], RidgeModel [27], ElasticNet [28], KNN [29], SVM [30], and NeoLsSVM [31]. We also evaluate DecisionTree, RandomForest [32], XGBoost [33], CatBoost [34], LightGBM [35], and xRFM [36]. Neural tabular models include MLP, RealMLP [25], and TabM [37]. Tabular foundation models comprise TabPFNv2.5 and RealTabPFNv2.5 [38], TabPFN-Wide [39], TabICLv2 [40], TabDPT [41], HyperFast [42], and iLTM [43]. 4 Implementation. All models use unified interface for preprocessing, training, hyperparameter optimization (HPO), and evaluation, with transformations fit only on training data and re-fit independently within each cross-validation fold. Default preprocessing uses numerical imputation, categorical encoding, and scaling, with model-specific overrides for methods with native missing-value, categorical, or internal preprocessing support (details in Appendix B). Hyperparameter Optimization. Each model is evaluated with default settings, and HPO is performed for all models except LinearModel and NeoLsSVM. HPO details and search spaces are provided in Appendix B.3. Optimization is constrained by wall-clock budgets of 6 hours per search for standard train/validation/test splits and 2 hours per outer fold for cross-validation. Main benchmark selection considers the default plus up to 100 attempted HPO configurations. These are equal wall-clock allowances, not equally exhaustive searches, and realized configuration counts are reported in Appendix G.1. Hyperparameters are selected based on validation performance using ROC-AUC for binary classification, log loss for multiclass classification, and MSE for regression tasks. For cross-validation, HPO is performed independently using inner validation within each outer folds training data, and test metrics are averaged across the five outer folds. Computational cost. The main benchmark required approximately 5,334 hours of cumulative logged runtime ( 0.61 serial wall-clock years), with 5% spent on default evaluations and 95% on tuning and selected-model refitting. 3.3 Evaluation We evaluate all methods on the benchmark splits introduced in Subsection 3.1, covering both fixedsplit and cross-validation settings. For cross-validation, we follow an outer-fold protocol and report mean standard deviation across folds. For fixed splits, we report performance on single held-out test set. For each dataset-model pair, we evaluate default configuration followed, where applicable, by model-specific hyperparameter optimization. Hyperparameters are selected solely based on validation performance, with the test set reserved for final evaluation. The selected configuration is then refit according to model-specific protocols, including training on combined training and validation data where applicable (see Appendix B.5). Final performance is evaluated on the held-out test set using the same task-specific primary metrics as HPO (Subsection 3.2). We summarize predictive performance using ranks within each dataset and mean and median scores after per-dataset min-max normalization  (Table 2)  . Normalized scores are also used in the pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Elo ratings are computed from within-dataset pairwise comparisons of primary test scores, respecting metric directionality. Details are provided in Appendix C. Pareto analyses compare Elo ratings with median training costs and inference times per 1,000 rows, including HPO in the training cost of Tuned configurations (Section 4).

sections.title: 4 Results and Analysis
sections.content: We compare models using normalized scores, dataset-level ranks, runtimes, and Elo ratings, and examine performance across biomedical domains and dataset size regimes. Rank-based analysis. For each dataset, models are ranked using the primary metric from Section 3.2 respecting metric directionality. We identify models appearing in the top-5 across datasets (Figure 1). Foundation models are most frequently represented, appearing in the top-5 for 88 datasets (vs. 57 for tree-based methods, 48 for neural methods, and 41 for classical baselines). Tree-based and classical methods also appear frequently among the top-performing models, and top-performing sets often include mix of foundation, tree-based, and baseline approaches, suggesting complementary strengths across biomedical tasks. Pairwise win rates across all datasets are reported in Appendix G.4. We restrict the main analysis to 21 models applicable to all 94 datasets, excluding classification-only models (TabPFN-Wide [39] and HyperFast [42]). As shown in Table 2, foundation models occupy several of the leading positions in the aggregate rankings across the benchmark. TabDPT [41] achieves the highest mean normalized score (0.865), while TabICLv2 [40] achieves the best mean rank (8.011). Neural-network-based methods also perform strongly. Advanced architectures such as RealMLP [25] and TabM [37] achieve mean normalized scores of 0.841 and 0.861, respectively, compared with 0.803 for the vanilla MLP baseline. TabM also achieves the third-best mean rank (8.170). Classical baselines such as ElasticNet [28], RidgeModel, and SVM [30] remain moderately competitive, with mean normalized scores of 0.765, 0.760, and 0.744, respectively. Their low inference costs, especially for the linear models, indicate that simpler models may still be efficient for resourceconstrained biomedical applications. Statistical Significance. Consistent with the work of TabZilla [10], we conducted statistical tests to assess whether observed differences in model performance are statistically significant. We first applied the Friedman test [44] to assess global differences in model rankings. The results indicate statistically significant differences between models at < 0.05. We then performed pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [45] with Holm-Bonferroni correction to control for multiple comparisons [46]. For this test, we used normalized scores because the comparison spans all four task types. Score selection and failure handling are detailed in Appendix C.1. Although the Friedman test identified statistically significant global differences, the subsequent Wilcoxon-Holm analysis revealed substantial overlap among the leading methods as shown in Figure 3. The ten models with the best mean ranks are TabICLv2, RealTabPFNv2.5, TabM, TabPFNv2.5, TabDPT, RealMLP, iLTM, CatBoost, xRFM, and LightGBM, with no statistically significant pairwise differences within this group. This suggests that differences in average ranks among top-performing methods do not necessarily correspond to statistically significant performance differences. At the same time, weaker-performing methods such as DecisionTree, NeoLsSVM, KNN and LinearModel performed significantly worse than the leading methods, indicating lower aggregate performance across heterogeneous biomedical datasets. To assess the sensitivity of model rankings to GPU memory, we also retry evaluations that failed with GPU out-of-memory errors on the benchmarks 24 GB A5500 GPUs using 80 GB A100 GPUs (Appendix G.3). For binary classification, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC rankings largely 8 agree (median Spearman ρ = 0.926), whereas the proper scoring rules log loss and Brier score favor TabICLv2 over RealTabPFNv2.5, the ROC-AUC leader (see Appendix H). Impact of Dataset Size and Dimensionality. We analyze dataset size and dimensionality regimes by splitting datasets at the medians of log10 sample size and feature count, yielding four regimes (Q1Q4). Figure 5 focuses on the 78 binary and multiclass classification tasks across all 23 models. This classification-only view additionally includes TabPFN-Wide, designed for high-dimensional classification [39], and HyperFast [42]. The corresponding analysis of all 94 tasks with the 21 models supporting classification, regression, and multi-target regression, excluding TabPFN-Wide and HyperFast, is reported in Appendix G.4.1. Foundation models achieve the highest Elo point estimate in all four classification regimes, with different models leading across regimes. TabICLv2 ranks first in the low-sample, low-feature (Q1) and high-sample, low-feature (Q3) regimes. In Q3, it is followed by the MLP-based RealMLP and TabM, then RealTabPFNv2.5 and iLTM (a foundation model whose meta-trained hypernetwork generates an MLP-based prediction network). RealTabPFNv2.5 leads the high-dimensional, lowsample-size (HDLSS) regime (Q2), followed by TabPFNv2.5 and TabPFN-Wide, which uses TabPFNv2 backbone. In the high-sample, high-feature regime (Q4), iLTM ranks first, followed by RealMLP and TabM. We additionally test whether principal component analysis (PCA) before TFM improves performance on high-dimensional inputs, comparing TabICLv2, TabPFNv2.5, and RealTabPFNv2.5 with their corresponding models without external PCA on all 36 datasets with more than 2,000 features (Appendix G.6). TabICLv2 benefits most, with 26 paired improvements and one successful evaluation where its non-PCA baseline failed, together covering 27 of 36 datasets. TabPFNv2.5 improves on 8 of 30 and obtains one new successful evaluation, and RealTabPFNv2.5 improves on 9 of 31 paired datasets. We hypothesize that the greater benefit for TabICLv2 might partly reflect its lack of native PCA/SVD preprocessing, whereas the TabPFN variants already combine feature subsampling with optional SVD-derived features. Reported correlation p-values are Holm-adjusted across all 180 metafeatureperformance comparisons. Figures 42 and 43 summarize these associations and compare families within dataset clusters (Appendix I). Pareto Frontiers. We construct Pareto frontiers to analyze trade-offs between Elo ratings and computational cost across models. Pareto optimality is defined over two objectives: minimizing median inference time or training cost per 1,000 rows and maximizing Elo rating. We also report domain-specific Pareto-optimal models in Appendix G.7. As shown in Figure 6, including HPO shifts the training-cost frontier toward Default configurations. Default LightGBM and RealTabPFNv2.5 combine competitive Elo ratings with low fitting cost, while Tuned RealTabPFNv2.5 reaches the highest Elo rating at greater training cost. For inference, Tuned LightGBM, CatBoost, and TabM offer favorable performance-latency trade-offs. LightGBM reaches near-frontier performance with inference times on the order of 102 seconds per 1k samples, several orders of magnitude faster than high-performing foundation models such as TabDPT and TabPFNv2.5.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we introduced TabBioMed, large-scale benchmark for biomedical tabular machine learning comprising 94 curated datasets across diverse clinical and biological domains. By standardizing the evaluation pipeline and benchmarking 23 models spanning four major algorithmic families, we demonstrated that no single model class universally dominates biomedical structured prediction. Foundation models occupy several of the leading positions in aggregate rankings, alongside advanced neural architectures such as TabM and RealMLP. TabDPT achieves the highest mean normalized score, TabICLv2 the best mean rank, and RealTabPFNv2.5 the highest Tuned Elo rating. Dataset properties and preprocessing affect these comparisons. Classical baselines are more competitive on datasets with higher feature-to-sample ratios. When accounting for computational efficiency, gradientboosted decision trees and classical linear models remain on the Pareto frontier. Including HPO shifts the training-cost frontier toward Default configurations, while Tuned LightGBM, CatBoost, and TabM offer favorable inference-time trade-offs. Ultimately, TabBioMed emphasizes that optimal model selection in biomedicine is highly contextand regime-dependent. We release our curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baseline implementations, and benchmark results. Limitations and Broader Impact. The benchmark is intended for comparative evaluation and methodological research rather than for direct clinical deployment or decision-making. Although TabBioMed spans 94 datasets across diverse biomedical domains, publicly available datasets may not fully represent real-world deployment settings, including clinical prediction over time [49], institution-specific pipelines [50], rare diseases [51], and underrepresented patient populations [52]. Our framework supports model-specific preprocessing, but may not fully capture specialized workflows commonly used across biomedical domains. Comparisons are conditional on the supplied tabular representations and do not establish the relative performance of alternative featurizations or modality-specific models. In addition, not all modeldataset evaluations completed successfully because of timeouts, memory exhaustion, or crashes. Strong benchmark performance should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness or deployment safety, as biomedical systems require additional considerations beyond predictive accuracy, including calibration, robustness, fairness, interpretability, prospective validation, and regulatory oversight. TabBioMed may positively impact biomedical machine learning research by improving transparency, reproducibility, and standardized comparison of modern machine learning approaches. At the same time, biomedical datasets may contain demographic, institutional, geographic, and socioeconomic biases inherited from the original data collection processes, potentially leading to unequal model performance across populations or healthcare systems. Benchmark overfitting, overreliance on leaderboard rankings, and the computational costs associated with large-scale benchmarking should also be considered.

sections.content: A.1 Curation Protocol at Glance Figure 7 summarizes dataset selection and preparation under the eligibility criteria in Section 3.1. 1. Identify public sources Clinical, molecular and omics studies and repositories. Record the source dataset or release. 2. Check task eligibility Explicit classification or regression target and data that can be represented as fixed-length feature vectors. 3. Select complementary tasks Cover domains and data regimes. Limit duplicate tasks and overlapping endpoints. exclude Exclude tasks requiring native sequence, image, graph or temporal modeling, or lacking defined supervised target. 4. Curate and unify Define labels, remove leakageprone variables and duplicates, preserve source-specific missingness and feature types. 7. Validate and document Check features, labels and partitions. Release source references, code, metadata and splits. 6. Define biomedical splits 5. Construct tabular features Define and store CV or fixed splits tailored to each dataset, e.g., molecular scaffold, sequence-cluster, patientor batch-based splits. Where needed, construct tabular features, e.g., molecular fingerprints, Coulomb matrices, aminoacid encodings, k-mer features and sequence embeddings. Figure 7: Dataset selection and curation workflow. Dataset-specific protocols take precedence over default splits. Model-specific preprocessing is fitted on training data only. Dataset characteristics and sources are described in Appendix A.2, and domain-specific curation and preprocessing in Appendix A.3. A.2 Dataset Inventory TabBioMed comprises 94 curated supervised learning datasets spanning diverse biomedical structured prediction tasks across molecular, clinical, and omics domains. The benchmark is designed to capture diversity while maintaining unified tabular prediction setting, where each sample is represented as fixed-dimensional feature vector derived from shared schema. Datasets were collected from several public repositories, published studies, and benchmark resources, including TALENT [13], OpenML [3], UCI Machine Learning Repository [53], PhysioNet [54], MoleculeNet [18], scikit-feature [55], PMLB [12], MLOmics [19], Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) [56], Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) [57], METABRIC [58], Metabolomics Workbench [59], MetaboLights [60], Hugging Face [61] repositories, and multiple genomics and single-cell resources. To reduce redundancy and improve benchmark diversity, representative subsets were selected when repositories contained highly overlapping tasks or correlated endpoints. For example, representative tasks were chosen from Tox21 [18, 62] and SIDER [18, 63] to maximize coverage across complementary prediction objectives while avoiding excessive duplication. Duplicate or near-duplicate tasks across repositories were similarly excluded where appropriate. Task abbreviations are defined as follows: Bin = binary classification, MultiC = multiclass classification, Reg = regression, and MultiReg = multi-target 22 regression. Across datasets, curation generally involved: Standardizing ingestion formats and metadata. Defining explicit predictive tasks. Removing leakage-prone or redundant variables. Preserving missing values as NaN unless domain-specific imputation was justified. Explicitly tracking feature types (numerical, categorical, sequence-derived). Creating fixed-split or cross-validation partitions, using 70/15/15 train/validation/test proportions by default for fixed-split tasks and preserving dataset-specific splitting requirements. Below we describe domain-specific curation procedures. A.3.1 Genomics Genomics datasets were constructed primarily from the gnomAD v3.1.2 callset combining 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) and Human Genome Diversity Project (HGDP) data [57, 81, 108, 109], supplemented by the TALENT DNA dataset [13, 14], and the coding-variant pathogenicity task vep_pathogenic_coding [82]. The 1KG+HGDP data provide whole-genome genotype information together with harmonized metadata describing sample sex, population labels, super-population labels, and geographic origin. Raw genotype data were initially processed using PLINK2 [110]. This included conversion from Variant Call Format (VCF) to PLINK 2s genotype format (PGEN), handling of pseudo-autosomal regions (PARs) using the hg38 definitions, sex-label correction, and reproducible subsampling of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Depending on the benchmark task, SNP subsets were selected either randomly or from consecutive genomic positions, allowing us to construct datasets with different feature dimensionalities while preserving reproducibility across runs. Subsequent processing used snputils [111]. Genotypes were converted to dosages by summing allele counts, yielding numerical features encoded as 0, 1, 2, or NaN, arranged in samples-by-features matrix. Samples were then aligned with the corresponding task labels, and samples without valid labels for given task were removed. Labels were constructed in task-specific manner. For sex prediction, binary sex labels were obtained from the available 1KG and HGDP sample metadata, and only chromosome variants were used as input features [112]. For ancestry prediction, labels were derived from the harmonized 1KG+HGDP metadata. Continental ancestry was formulated as seven-way classification task over the superpopulation categories AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, OCE, SAS, and WAS. Fine-grained ancestry prediction used subpopulation labels, such as GBR, CHB, or YRI, as multiclass targets. Geographic prediction was defined as multivariate regression task in which each sample was assigned latitude and longitude coordinates from the harmonized metadata. Finally, PCA prediction was defined as multivariate regression task using the first three ancestry principal components as targets. These coordinates were computed from genome-wide set of informative SNPs across autosomal chromosomes 122. From this unified genotype representation, we generated the following genomics benchmark datasets: Sexcheck datasets: sexcheck_chrX_50, and sexcheck_chrX_50k. These datasets predict sample sex from 50, 500, or 50,000 initially sampled chromosome SNPs, retaining 45, 441, and 17,118 features after preprocessing, respectively. For sexcheck_chrX_50k, we create three versions per individual by independently masking approximately 95% of genotype entries. All versions of an individual remain in the same partition. sexcheck_chrX_500, Continental ancestry datasets: and continental_50k_missing. These datasets use chromosome 22 SNPs to predict continental superpopulation labels. The continental_50k_missing variant randomly masks approximately 60% of genotype entries to evaluate robustness to incomplete genotype data. It retains one row per individual and the same train/validation/test assignments as continental_50k. continental_50k, continental_1k, Subpopulation ancestry datasets: subpop_1000_consec and subpop_50k. These datasets predict fine-grained population labels and differ in both feature dimensionality and SNP selection strategy, including consecutive-SNP variant. Geographic coordinate regression datasets: coords_1k and coords_50k. These datasets use genotype features to predict each samples geographic latitude and longitude. PCA regression datasets: pca_1k and pca_50k. These datasets use genotype features to predict the first three ancestry principal components. TALENT DNA dataset: dna task is three-class splice-site classification, included as an additional genomics task from the TALENT benchmark suite. Duplicate sequences were collapsed and sequence with conflicting labels was excluded before splitting. Variant pathogenicity dataset: vep_pathogenic_coding classifies coding singlenucleotide variants (SNVs) as ClinVar pathogenic or common gnomAD variants using only the surrounding GRCh38 reference sequence and the alternative allele. Allele-frequency, consequence-annotation, and genomic-position fields are excluded because they define or reveal the label. Splits hold out whole chromosomes, using Chr1, Chr4, and Chr21 for testing and Chr5, Chr6, and Chr11 for validation. 26 This design intentionally covers both classical genotype classification and structured representation learning tasks. In particular, the genomics subset spans binary classification, multiclass ancestry prediction, and multivariate regression, while also varying the number of SNP features, the genomic selection strategy, and the degree of missingness. A.3.2 Clinical and Healthcare Clinical datasets were gathered from heterogeneous repositories and unified through task-specific but consistent preprocessing. Common curation steps across EHR datasets included: Removal of leakage-prone variables (e.g. survival times, alternative outcomes). Harmonization of categorical clinical variables. Clinical grouping of diagnoses, such as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) categories. Explicit identification of categorical variables for downstream encoding. Subject-aware splitting when repeated patients were present. Several datasets required substantial dataset-specific curation. For example: VitalDB predicts in-hospital mortality using features available by the end of the operative/anesthesia case, including engineered indicators for devices and procedures, grouped diagnosis variables, missingness indicators, and duration-based features, with group-stratified splitting by patient. Hospital length of stay and ICU stay duration were excluded, and two impossible anesthesia durations were set to missing. MUSIC maps cause-of-death outcomes into four classes, excluding 11 patients lost to follow-up and 20 heart-transplant patients with unresolved outcomes. Predictors comprise clinical covariates, excluding follow-up variables and baseline ECG/Holter measurements. IACCD (Indwelling Arterial Catheter Clinical Dataset) is the separately released PhysioNet mimic2-iaccd dataset, available without credentialed access under the Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0.2 We removed redundant mortality indicators, administrative variables, and the whole-stay blood-gas test count (abg_count). Diabetes UCI predicts 30-day readmission at discharge. We retained the complete earliest encounter per patient, grouped the primary ICD-9 diagnosis and age bands, dropped secondary and tertiary diagnoses, and excluded hospice/death-related discharges following Strack et al. [113]. Admission type, discharge disposition, and admission source were treated as categorical features. Unmeasured HbA1c and glucose results form an explicit Not Measured category. Heart Disease UCI pools four source cohorts (Cleveland (USA), VA Long Beach (USA), Hungary, Switzerland) and binarizes disease severity. Zero cholesterol and resting blood pressure are treated as missing, and missing categorical values remain NaN for training-fitted imputation. Thyroid restores the released UCI feature values before TALENTs per-file standardization and marks binary flags as categorical. NHANES uses the CDC/NCHS National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 20132014 age-prediction subset (UCI-ID-887). Sex, physical activity, and diabetes responses are treated as categorical, with refused responses marked missing. Clinical datasets from TALENT [13] and OpenML [3] retained their source feature representations, with task-specific curation. In audiology, the binary target distinguishes the source diagnosis cochlear_age from all other diagnoses. Exact duplicate feature patterns were collapsed in audiology, blood-transfusion-service, and maternal_health_risk, and patterns with conflicting labels were excluded from the latter two. The same deduplication reduces CDC_Diabetes_Health_Indicators, derived from the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), from 253,680 to 226,342 records. In pima_diabetes, zero glucose, blood pressure, skinfold thickness, insulin, and BMI values are treated as missing. The redundant monetary feature, equal to 250 times donation frequency, was removed from blood-transfusion-service. In lymphography, the binary task distinguishes metastases from malignant lymph, retaining 142 2https://physionet.org/content/mimic2-iaccd/1.0/ 27 samples and excluding the normal and fibrosis cases. In Cardiovascular-Disease-dataset, duplicate feature patterns were collapsed, conflicting-label patterns were excluded, and outlier records violating fixed blood-pressure and anthropometric plausibility bounds were removed. Two clinical tasks were obtained from PMLB [12] and verified against their original UCI releases. dermatology predicts six erythemato-squamous diagnoses from clinical and histopathological findings after biopsy. The original numeric ages are used, preserving eight unknown ages as missing. spectf predicts normal versus abnormal cardiac single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) from 44 image summaries. We removed 82 duplicate copies, recovering the corrected 267-patient UCI cohort. We pooled its source training and test files for five-fold outer cross-validation with three-fold inner validation, as for dermatology. A.3.3 Drug Discovery and Molecular Properties Drug discovery and molecular-property datasets were primarily sourced from MoleculeNet [18], supplemented with additional tasks from OpenML [3] and TALENT [13, 14]. From MoleculeNet, we select QM8, QM9, SIDER, Tox21, HIV, and ESOL. These datasets are chosen to ensure coverage across the main molecular property categories defined in MoleculeNet, namely quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics, and physiology. QM8 and QM9 are selected over earlier benchmarks such as QM7 to cover larger molecular collections and broader range of quantum-chemical properties [18]. QM9 in particular covers more complex molecules and is widely adopted in molecular machine learning [114, 115]. ESOL is selected as the representative physical chemistry regression task, as it is one of the most widely used molecular regression benchmarks and is consistently included across major evaluation frameworks such as MoleculeNet and OGB [116]. HIV is included as the representative biophysics single-task classification dataset, PCBA and MUV are discarded due to their excessive number of tasks and samples, and HIV is preferred over PDBbind and BACE for its larger sample size, given that small datasets are already represented by SIDER. Tox21 is chosen to include toxicity classification dataset over ToxCast, as it is more widely adopted and was central to the landmark Tox21 Data Challenge [62] in machine learning for drug discovery. SIDER is selected as the representative adverse drug reaction dataset, containing approved drugs and their reported adverse drug reactions. Except for ESOL and HIV, which contain single prediction target, all remaining datasets consist of multiple labels. For the quantum chemistry targets, we include only E1CC2 and f1CC2, as CC2 corresponds to the reference level of theory used in the original dataset, while alternative computational methods are primarily included for comparison purposes. For electronic structure and thermodynamic targets, we select the energy gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), and Gibbs free energy at 298 K. These targets capture distinct aspects of molecular behavior, including electronic excitation, reactivity, and thermodynamic stability, and were selected based on both physical interpretability and low redundancy, as assessed through correlation and clustering analysis. For Tox21, we select three tasks spanning both regulatory panels and range of difficulty levels: NR-AhR, NR-ER and SR-MMP. For SIDER, we select two adverse-effect endpoints: gastrointestinal disorders and nervous system disorders. For the QM8 and QM9 datasets from MoleculeNet [18], we generate random 70/15/15 train/validation/test splits. For the remaining datasets (SIDER, Tox21, HIV, and ESOL), we employ scaffold splitting [18], following growing consensus in recent literature that scaffold splitting provides more realistic and challenging evaluation setting by better testing model generalization across chemical structures [117119]. All datasets use consistent 70/15/15 train/validation/test split. Regression targets for QM8, QM9, and ESOL are z-scored using training-split statistics. Featurization is adapted to the nature of each task. For quantum chemistry datasets (QM8 and QM9), we use the Coulomb matrix representation [120], computed using the DeepChem package [121]. Coulomb matrices explicitly encode nuclear charges and interatomic distances, whereas purely topological fingerprints such as extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP) omit explicit threedimensional geometry [18]. For the remaining datasets, we use binary Morgan fingerprints [122], widely adopted baseline in molecular machine learning due to their strong empirical performance across diverse property prediction tasks. Radius is set to 2, and initial fingerprint dimensionality is set to 1024 for datasets with more than 2,000 samples and 2048 otherwise. 28 The two tasks from TALENT and OpenML, QSAR_biodegradation and bioresponse, provide precomputed molecular descriptors without molecular structures in the releases we use, so both use random 70/15/15 splits. QSAR_biodegradation predicts ready biodegradability from 41 descriptors. Three duplicate descriptor rows with matching labels were collapsed before stratified splitting, leaving 1,051 molecules. bioresponse predicts binary biological response for 3,751 molecules from molecular descriptors. A.3.4 Metabolomics Metabolomics datasets were assembled from clinical metabolomics studies in Metabolomics Workbench and MetaboLights [21, 22], together with volatile organic compound mass-spectrometry datasets from TabPFN-VOCS [84]. The clinical subset follows prior metabolomics benchmark selections [21, 22] and includes the studies ST000369, ST000496, ST001000, ST001047, MTBLS136, MTBLS161, and MTBLS404, formulated as study-specific binary classification tasks. For each study, the relevant analysis matrix was selected, sample identifiers were aligned with phenotype annotations, samples without valid labels were removed, and labels were encoded as 0 and 1. For ST000496, the paired preand post-treatment samples from 50 patients are grouped by patient in both outer and inner cross-validation, including the final-fit validation holdout, and patient identifiers are excluded from the features. The TabPFN-VOCS subset comprises proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTRToF-MS) measurements of chewing-gum formulations (Gum1_s), roasted hazelnut paste (Noc_s), and fungal cultures (PT-Mush21). The first two are regression tasks and the third is classification task. Source IDs for Gum1_s and Noc_s, and biological-strain IDs for PT-Mush21, define five grouped outer folds that test each sample once. These datasets cover agrifood and fungal-culture settings, predicting component-1 concentration in chewing-gum formulations, hazelnut roasting time, and fungal species, respectively. Limited strain support requires two inner folds for PT-Mush21, while the regression tasks use three. For the clinical metabolomics datasets, measurement features were transformed using log1p to reduce right-skewness, heteroscedasticity, and the large dynamic range typical of mass-spectrometry data. Because appropriate normalization depends on the measurement process, dataset characteristics, and downstream analysis [123, 8], we did not impose an additional uniform sample-wise normalization step across the clinical metabolomics datasets. A.3.5 Systems Biology The systems biology benchmark uses five cancer-cohort datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), curated by MLOmics [19], where multiple omics modalities are provided as separate feature matrices. For each dataset, modalities were first loaded independently and aligned using shared sample identifiers to ensure correct sample correspondence across data types. The aligned modalities were then concatenated into single unified multi-omics feature table. For GS-LGG, methylation beta values were reconstructed from TCGA via UCSC Xena using patient barcodes and verified CpG identifiers, retaining the 4,705 source probes assayed on the HumanMethylation450 platform.3 Features were coerced into numeric format. All resulting features are treated as continuous numerical variables, and no additional feature engineering is applied beyond modality-level fusion. A.3.6 Single-Cell Omics Single-cell datasets were collected from Tahoe-100M [107], the mouse gastrulation atlas [104], scUnified [124], and the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas (HNOCA) [103]. Appropriate normalization depends on the downstream analysis task [125]. In TabBioMed, we retained source-specific expression representations without imposing common normalization or batch-correction pipeline. Gene filtering and selection used training cells only, and dataset-specific procedures are described below. From Tahoe-100M, we generated cell-line classification datasets and cell-cycle regression task. The included classification datasets, tahoe_cell_name_500, tahoe_cell_name_1000, and tahoe_cell_name_5000, are three feature-width variants predicting cell-line identity using the top 500, 1,000, or 5,000 genes selected by Pearson residuals on training cells. Train, validation, and test 3https://tcga.xenahubs.net/download/TCGA.LGG.sampleMap/HumanMethylation450.json 29 splits were constructed using held-out plates, with random subsampling to obtain consistent split sizes. The tahoe_g2m_score dataset is regression task predicting the G2/M cell-cycle score using the same feature-selection strategy. The tahoe_batch_integration_14plates dataset predicts the plate of origin of each cell: 2,000 cells were randomly sampled from each of the 14 plates and randomly split 70/15/15 into training, validation, and test sets, and 5,000 genes were selected by Pearson residuals on the training cells. From HNOCA, we included hnoca_cells30, which predicts the 30 most frequent harmonized level4 cell types. Publicationcell-line connected components were assigned to disjoint training, validation, and test sets, followed by class-stratified subsampling to 70,000/15,000/15,000 cells. We selected 22,000 genes by Pearson-residual variance using only the training cells counts_lengthnorm layer, and features retain the source log-transformed counts per million (CPM), log(1 + CPM). The sc_gastrulation_stage task predicts recorded embryonic collection day from the mouse gastrulation atlas [104], using embryo-pool-disjoint splits and training-only gene selection. From scUnified, sc_muris_age classifies recorded mouse age (3, 18, or 24 months), and sc_muris_celltype predicts nine released kidney cell-type annotations [105]. The sc_muraro_celltype task predicts eight released human pancreas cell-type annotations, excluding three epsilon cells [106]. These tasks use stratified cell-level splits, retaining kidney raw counts and released pancreas expression values after removing training-constant genes, and identifiers and other annotations are excluded from predictors. A.3.7 Proteomics Proteomics benchmarks combine quantitative mass-spectrometry datasets with protein sequencebased prediction tasks. The mass-spectrometry subset is derived from the CPTAC UCEC endometrial cancer cohort [96], using the UMich protein-abundance and aliquot-to-patient mapping tables and MSSM clinical_Pan-cancer.May2022 annotations from Zenodo archive v41 [97]. Tables were accessed using the cptac package version 1.5.14. Patient matching and histology selection yield 101 distinct tumor patients (80 endometrioid and 21 serous), with one proteomics profile per patient, for the binary cptac_histology task. The general preprocessing pipeline removes constant or entirely missing columns, retaining 12,592 features with missing measurements preserved as NaN. The PMLB/UCI ecoli task predicts five protein subcellular locations from 327 proteins. Protein identifiers are excluded from features. From the collection InstaDeepAI/true-cds-protein-tasks hosted on Hugging Face, we include three protein sequence regression tasks also represented in the PEER benchmark [126]: true_melting_point, true_betalactamase_unique, and true_fluorescence. These tasks evaluate complementary aspects of protein sequence understanding, including thermostability, mutational fitness, and fluorescence. We used the train/validation/test splits provided by the benchmark collection. The source coding DNA sequences were first translated to amino-acid sequences, excluding sequences with internal stop codons. Melting point and beta-lactamase prediction were represented using mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings [127] from esm2_t12_35M_UR50D, computed with the protenc Python package, whereas fluorescence prediction used TF-IDF features computed from amino-acid 3-mers. From Proteinea [99], we include proteinea_solubility, binary protein-solubility task using the DeepSol dataset [98]. We preserve the released train/validation/test partitions (62,478/6,942/2,001 sequences). Protein sequences were represented using normalized amino-acid 3-mer frequencies, yielding fixed-length feature representation over all possible 3-mers from the standard amino-acid alphabet. From AVIDa, we include binary binding prediction tasks for nanobodies, the variable domains of heavy-chain-only antibodies (VHHs), against hIL6 [92, 93], hTNFa [94], and SARS-CoV-2 [95]. The included datasets are avida_hil6_onehot, avida_htnfa_onehot, avida_htnfa_3mer, avida_htnfa_esm2, and avida_sarscov2_3mer. These variants intentionally cover multiple sequence encoding strategies: padded amino-acid token encodings, TF-IDF amino-acid 3-mer features, and mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings. For paired sequence inputs, such as nanobody-antigen pairs, representations were computed separately for each sequence and concatenated. Data-dependent encodings, such as TF-IDF vocabularies and padding lengths, are fitted on training rows only. For hIL6 and hTNFa, splits are VHH-family-disjoint: nanobody sequences are clustered with CD-HIT 30 and whole families are assigned to the training, validation, or test set. For SARS-CoV-2, we keep the provided split by alpaca, draw validation from the training alpaca as whole VHH families, and remove training and validation pairs that exactly match test nanobody-antigen pair. A.3.8 Transcriptomics Seven transcriptomics datasets were sourced from scikit-feature [55], alongside TOX_171 from GEO (GDS968/GSE1725), accessed through the same collection. These eight datasets were selected to represent both binary and multi-class classification tasks across diverse cancer and gene expression profiling studies. These raw inputs were converted into unified structure where gene expression features (X) and corresponding labels (y) were extracted, with label encoding applied when necessary. For TOX_171, the outer and inner cross-validation folds are grouped by donor. The METABRIC task [58] predicts recorded histological grades 13 from primary breast-tumor expression in 1,892 distinct patients (169, 771, and 952 per grade). We exclude 88 expression-profiled patients without recorded grade and retain 20,603 source expression measurements at their supplied log2 intensities. Evaluation uses patient-disjoint, grade-stratified data splits. The final benchmark contains curated datasets spanning eight biomedical domains and four task types as shown in Figure 2. We provide additional visualizations of key dataset properties in TabBioMed, including sample size, feature dimensionality, feature-type composition, missingness, and class distribution in Figure 8. Figure 8: Dataset Characteristics of the TabBioMed Benchmark. Distributions of key dataset properties, including number of samples, number of features, feature-type composition, missingness, and number of classes (for multiclass classification datasets only).

sections.content: The modeling pipeline follows unified experimental framework designed to ensure consistency among 23 models across four families ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern tabular foundation models and deep learning architectures (see Table 12). The entire process is organized into three main stages: dataset preprocessing, training with HPO, and final refitting with evaluation. While shared pipeline governs all models, each model class selectively overrides components of preprocessing, training behavior, and refitting logic depending on its inductive biases and internal learning mechanisms. This design allows fair comparison while respecting 31 model-specific requirements such as native categorical handling, internal normalization strategies, or validation-dependent optimization. At global level, preprocessing consists of three steps: Missing values in numerical features are handled only when required by the model. By default, numerical imputation uses K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) imputation with five neighbors, fitted on the training split and applied to all splits. The default encoding for nonbinary categorical features is one-hot encoding, with model-specific alternatives described below. Scaling is fitted at training time and applied only to non-categorical, non-binary features using either StandardScaler or QuantileTransformer depending on model configuration. Model-specific Preprocessing. All Baseline models listed in Table 12, along with MLP, rely on the full preprocessing pipeline. DecisionTree uses categorical encoding without feature scaling or missing-value imputation. Random Forest uses categorical encoding and native numerical missing-value handling without feature scaling. RealMLP uses mean imputation with missingness indicators, while categorical encoding, robust scaling, and smooth clipping are handled internally by the model. xRFM uses mean imputation with missingness indicators followed by one-hot encoding of categorical features and standardization of numerical features. Gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) models (XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) do not use standard preprocessing. Missing values are handled natively without imputation. For categorical variables, XGBoost requires integer encoding, LightGBM uses internally supported categorical indices, and CatBoost directly consumes raw string categorical features. No feature scaling is applied. Tabular foundation models including TabPFNv2.5, TabPFN-Wide, RealTabPFNv2.5, TabICLv2, TabDPT, HyperFast and iLTM generally rely on internal preprocessing, with exceptions such as label encoding of categorical features for TabDPT. Missing values are handled internally, categorical features follow model-specific encoding procedures, and external feature scaling is disabled in favor of internal normalization mechanisms. The hybrid neural model TabM partially modifies the standard pipeline. Missing values are imputed using mean imputation, and categorical variables are encoded using label encoding instead of one-hot encoding. Following the official TabM recipe, non-binary numerical features are transformed with QuantileTransformer fitted on the training split, and the benchmarks generic scaler is disabled to avoid redundant second transformation. 32 B.2 Training and Hyperparameter Optimization Details Training is orchestrated through unified experiment runner that supports both default baselines and hyperparameter optimization. The pipeline distinguishes between three execution modes: default baseline evaluation, HPO trials, and final test evaluation of the validation-selected configuration. For final test evaluation of the default baseline, models are initialized using their predefined hyperparameters and trained either on the training split alone or on merged training-validation set. The decision depends on whether model uses validation data during fitting. Models without internal validation mechanisms are trained on the combined train-validation split to maximize data usage. In contrast, models that rely on early stopping or internal validation strictly train on the training set while reserving the validation split for monitoring. During hyperparameter optimization, each trial executes full training cycle but restricts evaluation to the validation set. Importantly, test data are never used during HPO. The training configuration during HPO explicitly disables train-validation merging to ensure strict separation between training and evaluation. Configurations are compared using the same validation data. For validation scoring, the default configuration is fitted on the training partition without train-validation merging and evaluated on the same validation data as the sampled configurations, with ties resolved in favor of the default. Experiments are run using Slurm-based pipeline. Each run is allocated up to 10 CPU cores, 128 GB RAM, and one NVIDIA RTX A5500 GPU when applicable (primarily for neural and foundation models, while tree-based models use CPU unless GPU execution is supported). Each Slurm job has 24-hour wall-clock limit. Model selection, including validation evaluation of the default configuration, has budget of six hours per fixed-split search or two hours per outer cross-validation fold. Standalone Default baseline evaluations and final refits (outside the HPO search) may exceed this selection budget, subject to the remaining Slurm job time. Trial histories and progress reports are saved incrementally for reproducibility and fault tolerance, and completed evaluations retain test predictions. We record training and inference times as wall-clock measurements for both default and tuned models, along with evaluation metadata. Failed or resourceexceeded runs are retained as missing evaluations. In downstream analysis, we report complete-case results and analyses where missing entries are imputed using the default Random Forest result on the same dataset. Tree-based models exhibit more diverse behavior. Random Forest operates without validation dependency and follows standard training procedures. We ran CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost with up to 10,000 boosting iterations together with early stopping on the validation set, following the implementations used in AutoGluon and TabArena [4]. xRFM is tree-structured kernel method, rather than conventional tree ensemble. It combines tree-based partitioning with kernel-based leaf predictors and uses validation-based early stopping. For family-level analyses, we group xRFM with tree-based models to retain four broad categories without introducing separate category for single method. These validation-dependent models therefore bypass train-validation merging entirely across all stages. MLP-based architectures, including MLP, RealMLP, TabM, and also iLTM (for its generated target network, not for the meta-learned hypernetwork), follow validation-dependent optimization regimes. These models typically employ epoch-based training loops with validation monitoring for early stopping or performance tracking. For instance, MLP uses custom PyTorch training loop with validation-based convergence control, while TabM uses internal early stopping. For these models, both hyperparameter optimization and final refit phases keep training and validation partitions separate. TabM removes numerical features with fewer than two unique values in the training partition before applying its quantile transformation and fitting the network. The same feature selection is applied to validation and test data, avoiding degenerate constant-feature embeddings. In-context learning models introduce different training dynamics. The TabPFN-family models evaluated here (TabPFNv2.5, TabPFN-Wide and RealTabPFNv2.5) do not undergo gradient-based training during benchmark evaluation. Instead, they perform inference using pretrained models conditioned on the input context. Consequently, their training phase is effectively preprocessing and inference setup step, although Optuna still tunes inference configuration parameters. TabICLv2 and TabDPT similarly use in-context learning, with training reduced to configuring inference behavior 33 rather than parameter optimization. For these models, validation data guide configuration selection without updating the pretrained weights. Training and validation data are then merged into the context pool for final test evaluation. B.3 Hyperparameter Optimization In this section, we describe the hyperparameter optimization details used for tuning the models evaluated in the TabBioMed benchmark. The majority of the search spaces are adopted or adapted from TabArena [4]. This includes the search spaces for Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, KNN, RealMLP, xRFM, TabM, TabDPT, TabICLv2, TabPFNv2.5 and RealTabPFNv2.5, including search spaces added to the official TabArena GitHub repository after its original publication. LinearModel and NeoLsSVM are evaluated using their default settings without external HPO. LinearModel is unpenalized, while Lasso, Ridge, and ElasticNet cover regularized linear models. NeoLsSVM automatically selects its regularization internally. We use the following model-specific search spaces and adaptations: Baseline Models: For Lasso, Ridge and ElasticNet, we defined search spaces covering regularization strengths and scaling options. For SVM and DecisionTree, the search spaces were adapted from TabZilla [10], with additional DecisionTree parameters for the splitting strategy and minimum split and leaf sizes. Other Foundation Models: For the remaining foundation models, we use the following search spaces and configurations: For HyperFast we adopted the recommended search space, and for iLTM we evaluate up to 25 recommended configurations from the official GitHub repository. TabPFN-Wide: We aimed to closely match TabArenas TabPFNv2.5 search space while adapting it to the specific version of the tabpfn package required by TabPFNWides implementation. Search-space adaptations: For XGBoost, we lowered the minimum min_child_weight from 103 to 105 and additionally tuned scale_pos_weight log-uniformly over [0.1, 10]. For TabM, we implemented TabArenas existing mixtures for weight_decay and dropout using conditional parameters, preserving their sampling distributions. B.5 Final Refit and Evaluation In general, the refitting procedure re-executes training using the best hyperparameters identified during HPO. However, the handling of training and validation data differs significantly across model families. For models that do not use validation during training, the final refit is performed on merged training and validation dataset. This includes linear models, tree-based models such as Random Forest, kernel methods such as SVM and NeoLsSVM, and foundation models such as TabPFN, TabICLv2, and TabDPT. This merging maximizes training data availability since these models do not use validation data during fitting. 41 Conversely, models that depend on validation during training explicitly avoid merging training and validation data in the final stage. This includes boosting models (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), all neural architectures (MLP, RealMLP, TabM), xRFM, HyperFast, and iLTM. For these models, the validation set remains separate for monitoring and model selection. In-context learning models (TabPFNv2.5, RealTabPFNv2.5, TabPFN-Wide, TabICLv2, and TabDPT) do not update pretrained weights during final evaluation. Instead, they rerun preprocessing and inference setup using the validation-selected configuration and the merged training-validation context. xRFM follows hybrid procedure: it reinitializes internal preprocessing components and retrains its kernel-based representation with the optimal configuration. sections.title: C Benchmark Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate all models using task-specific primary metrics defined by the nature of the prediction problem: Binary classification: Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC, higher is better) Multiclass classification: Logarithmic Loss (log loss, lower is better) Regression and multi-target regression: Mean Squared Error (MSE, lower is better) These metrics serve as the primary evaluation signal across all datasets and are used consistently in all downstream analyses. Fixed-Split Evaluation. For datasets with predefined train/validation/test splits, models are trained on the training set, tuned on the validation set, and evaluated on the held-out test set. We report test performance corresponding to the selected configuration (default or hyperparameter-tuned), with the test set strictly reserved for final evaluation. Cross-Validation Evaluation. For datasets evaluated under cross-validation, we use five outer folds. Hyperparameters are selected independently within each outer folds non-test samples by the mean validation score across three inner folds, reduced to two when class or group support requires it. For 43 automatically generated splits, the stored final-fit training, final-fit validation, and outer-test partitions contain approximately 70%, 10%, and 20% of the dataset, respectively. Dataset-specific predefined splits are preserved. The selected configuration is then refitted on the combined training and validation data, except for models that require validation data during fitting, which retain the separate validation subset, and evaluated on the held-out outer test fold. Final performance is reported as the mean test score across the five outer folds. Standard deviation across folds is also computed and reported where applicable, but is not used for aggregation or ranking. This yields single dataset-level performance value per model configuration for aggregate comparisons. Normalized Scores. To enable comparison across heterogeneous datasets and metrics, we apply per-dataset minmax normalization. For each dataset d, let sm,d denote the test performance of model m, and let Md be the set of evaluated models on that dataset. The normalized score sm,d is defined as: For metrics where higher values are better: sm,d = sm,d minmMd sm,d maxmMd sm,d minmMd sm,d . For metrics where lower values are better: sm,d = maxmMd sm,d sm,d maxmMd sm,d minmMd sm,d . This transformation yields scores in [0, 1], where 1 corresponds to the best-performing model and 0 corresponds to the worst-performing model on each dataset. The normalization is performed independently per dataset and is intended for comparative analysis within the benchmark rather than as an absolute performance measure. C.1 Statistical comparison across all datasets. The CD analysis includes all 94 datasets and the 21 models applicable to every task type. For each model and dataset, we use the Tuned test result when available, otherwise the Default test result. Models without HPO use Default results. For cross-validation datasets, each variants test metric is averaged across all outer folds and is considered available only when every fold has valid result. Successful results are min-max normalized within the 21-model comparison using the formulas above. When neither variant has complete test result, the model receives normalized score of 0 and ties with the worst successful model. Per-dataset ranks use average ties, and all datasets are retained. Friedman tests use these ranks, and two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests use the normalized scores, with Holm-Bonferroni correction across all model pairs at α = 0.05. C.2 Elo analysis. The main Elo analysis evaluates Default and Tuned configurations as separate competitors for the same 21 models used in Table 2. LinearModel and NeoLsSVM are Default-only, giving 40 eligible configurations. For cross-validation datasets, configurations primary test metric is averaged across every expected outer fold before comparisons are formed. configuration with an incomplete outerfold evaluation has no dataset-level score. Each dataset contributes equally, and pairwise comparisons respect the task-specific metric direction, and ties count as half win for each competitor. The main analysis includes all 94 datasets, replacing each missing Default or Tuned score with the Default Random Forest score on the same dataset. This imputes 59 configurationdataset entries. The complete-case analysis uses the 79 datasets with valid scores for every eligible configuration. Default and Tuned remain separate competitors under both analyses. Ratings are fitted jointly under the Bradley-Terry model using logistic regression with weak ℓ2 regularization (C = 106). We draw 200 bootstrap resamples of datasets with replacement, refit the ratings, and use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for 95% confidence intervals. The additive offset that anchors the Default Random Forest point estimate to 1000 Elo is also applied to the bootstrap interval endpoints. The regime and feature-count figures use one competitor per model. For each dataset, they use complete Tuned test result, otherwise the models complete Default result. Only when both are 44 unavailable is the Default Random Forest score used. The RandomForest model competitor is anchored at 1000 in these figures.

sections.title: E Dependence Among Related Datasets
sections.content: Several TabBioMed tasks are derived from the same observations or from the same source collection. Examples include the twelve genotype tasks built from the 1KG+HGDP callset or the endpoints selected from MoleculeNet. Treating all 94 tasks as independent evidence could therefore give additional weight to some sources. We identified these relations in the processed data, verified them against the benchmark results, and recomputed the leaderboards with group weighting and leave-one-group-out exclusion. Dataset groups. We distinguish two levels of dependence. Same-X groups contain tasks derived from shared or overlapping observations (individuals, cells, molecules, patients, or sequence pairs), potentially differing in prediction targets, feature representations, or retained samples. Source families group tasks by data-generation project, curated collection, or domain-specific repository, without requiring shared observations. This broader grouping tests sensitivity to source composition. Generic multi-domain hosts (UCI, OpenML, TALENT, PMLB, PhysioNet, and Hugging Face) are not treated as families. Each grouping is partition of the 94 tasks in which ungrouped tasks are singletons, giving 71 same-X units and 42 source-family units. The two levels are analyzed separately. Table 36 lists every group. Weighting and exclusion. We use the 21 models supporting all 94 tasks. For weighting, each task in group receives weight 1/g in the pairwise comparisons, so every group, including singletons, counts as single task, and bootstrap intervals resample whole groups. sections.content: We present additional analyses to complement the main benchmark results, covering robustness across tasks, efficiency trade-offs, and structural patterns in model performance. These analyses operate on the same underlying evaluation framework described in Section 3.3 and Appendix C, but differ in aggregation level (global, task-specific, and domain-specific views). G.1 Realized HPO Budgets and Overtuning Diagnostics Realized search effort. Figure 19 reveals clear performance hierarchy across the evaluated models. Foundation-style tabular architectures, particularly RealTabPFNv2.5, TabPFNv2.5, and TabICLv2, occupy the leading positions alongside TabM and achieve consistently high pairwise win rates against most competing methods. RealTabPFNv2.5 achieves win rates of 51.1% against TabPFNv2.5, 45.2% against TabICLv2, and 58.5% against TabDPT. Each feature-count group includes datasets with widely varying sample sizes. This analysis complements the joint feature-count and sample-size analysis presented in Figure 21 by examining how relative model performance and execution reliability vary across feature-dimensionality regimes. Figure 23 presents the calibrated Elo ratings of the 21 evaluated models across the three feature regimes. On low-feature datasets, tabular foundation models occupy the leading positions, with TabICLv2 achieving the highest Elo rating (1,263.9), followed by RealTabPFNv2.5 (1,180.9) and TabPFNv2.5 (1,157.8). TabICLv2 completes all 31 datasets, while RealTabPFNv2.5 and TabPFNv2.5 each achieve completion rate of 96.77%. similar pattern emerges in the medium-feature regime, where TabICLv2 maintains the highest Elo rating (1,311.7), followed by iLTM (1,226.8), TabPFNv2.5 (1,187.4), RealMLP (1,183.3), and RealTabPFNv2.5 (1,181.9). These results indicate that tabular foundation models remain highly competitive on datasets with low to moderate feature dimensionality. In the high-feature regime, the relative ordering changes substantially, with neural networks and tree-based methods becoming more prominent. RealMLP achieves the highest Elo rating (1,147.5), followed by CatBoost (1,146.8), TabM (1,145.6), TabDPT (1,141.8), and LightGBM (1,132.5). RealMLP, TabM, TabDPT and LightGBM complete all 32 datasets, while CatBoost completes 31 of 32. sections.content: H.1 Motivation and Evaluation Protocol The primary evaluation metric for binary classification in TabBioMed is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), consistent with established tabular benchmarking protocols. However, ROC-AUC primarily measures discriminative ability and does not directly assess the quality of predicted probabilities. In biomedical classification tasks, particularly those involving substantial class imbalance, complementary metrics can provide additional information about minority-class performance and the reliability of predicted probabilities. To examine the sensitivity of benchmark conclusions to the choice of evaluation metric, we extend the binary classification analysis to include the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), binary log loss, Brier score, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). PR-AUC, computed as average precision, provides complementary discrimination-oriented assessment that is particularly informative for 73 imbalanced classification tasks. Binary log loss and Brier score are strictly proper scoring rules that evaluate the quality of predicted probabilities, whereas ECE provides descriptive estimate of probability calibration. For each model and dataset, we use complete Tuned test results when available, otherwise complete Default results, and use the same variant for all five metrics. Crossvalidation results require all five outer test folds and are averaged across folds. Modeldataset pairs without either complete variant are excluded from this analysis. For each evaluation metric, models are ranked separately within each dataset. Higher values indicate better performance for ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, whereas lower values are preferred for binary log loss, Brier score, and ECE. Model performance is subsequently summarized using mean and median ranks across datasets. To assess ranking consistency, we compare the model rankings obtained under each alternative metric against those obtained using ROC-AUC. Agreement is quantified using Spearmans rank correlation coefficient (ρ) and Kendalls rank correlation coefficient (τ ). We additionally report the frequency of changes in the dataset-level top-ranked model and the Jaccard similarity between the sets of the three highest-ranked models under each pair of metrics. The analysis includes 48 binary classification datasets. To investigate the influence of class imbalance, datasets are stratified according to their class imbalance ratio (IR), using threshold of IR = 2. This yields 25 relatively balanced datasets (IR 2) and 23 imbalanced datasets (IR > 2). Calibration Evaluation. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is computed using the predicted probabilities of the positive class. Predictions are partitioned into = 15 equal-width bins over [0, 1]. Within each bin, calibration error is the absolute difference between the observed positiveclass frequency and the mean predicted probability. ECE is the sample-weighted average of these discrepancies: ECE = (cid:88) b=1 Sb> Sb (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) 1 Sb (cid:88) iSb yi 1 Sb (cid:88) iSb (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) , ˆpi (1) where Sb is the set of samples assigned to bin b, is the total number of samples, yi {0, 1} is the observed binary label, and ˆpi [0, 1] is the predicted probability of the positive class. Empty bins contribute zero. ECE is used as complementary descriptive calibration diagnostic rather than as standalone measure of overall probabilistic performance. Accordingly, conclusions regarding predicted probability quality are primarily supported by the strictly proper scoring rules, binary log loss and Brier score, with ECE providing additional evidence about estimated calibration. The aggregate rankings show that RealTabPFNv2.5 achieves the lowest mean rank under both ROCAUC (6.30) and PR-AUC (5.85), indicating that the leading model remains unchanged across the two discrimination-oriented metrics. TabPFNv2.5 also maintains competitive rankings under both metrics, with mean ranks of 6.87 and 6.29, respectively. H.3 Agreement Between Alternative Evaluation Metrics To evaluate the robustness of model rankings to the choice of evaluation metric, we compare rankings obtained using PR-AUC, binary log loss, Brier score, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) against the primary ROC-AUC-based rankings. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC exhibit strong ranking agreement, with median Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.926 and Kendall correlation of τ = 0.800. This indicates that models performing well under ROC-AUC generally maintain favorable relative rankings under PR-AUC. The dataset-level top-ranked model changes on 19 of the 48 datasets (39.6%), indicating that strong overall ranking agreement does not necessarily imply identical model selection for individual datasets. The median top-3 Jaccard similarity of 0.500 further indicates partial overlap among the highest-ranked models. Agreement is more moderate when ROC-AUC is compared with binary log loss and Brier score. Binary log loss yields median correlations of ρ = 0.608 and τ = 0.452, while Brier score produces ρ = 0.674 and τ = 0.520. To further examine the relationship between class imbalance and ranking consistency, Figure 41 shows the dataset-level Spearman rank correlations between ROC-AUC and each alternative evaluation metric as function of the class imbalance ratio. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC maintain high median ranking agreement in both relatively balanced and imbalanced datasets (0.949 and 0.917, respectively), although Figure 41 shows lower agreement for several highly imbalanced datasets. Larger decreases occur for binary log loss (0.705 to 0.489) and Brier score (0.774 to 0.498).
